title: Communication Foundations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Communication is the transfer of meaning, not just information — the message received matters more than the message sent. The Shannon-Weaver model: sender → encoding → channel → decoding → receiver, with noise at every stage. Mehrabian's research on emotional communication: tone and body language carry disproportionate weight when words and delivery conflict. Active listening is the highest-leverage skill: listening to understand, not to reply. The curse of knowledge — experts forget what it's like not to know, and communicate over people's heads.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A manager says 'we need this soon.' The employee hears 'this week'; the manager meant 'today.' The words transferred; the meaning didn't. Specificity ('by 3pm today') eliminates the gap. Most communication failures are precision failures, not effort failures.

PRACTICE: 1) Rewrite three vague requests as specific ones. 2) Identify one instance where you assumed shared context that wasn't shared. 3) Practice reflecting back what someone said before responding.

title: Clarity, Structure & Persuasion
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The Pyramid Principle (Minto): lead with the answer, then support it — never build up to the point. BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) is the military version. The Rule of Three: humans retain three points, not seven. Signposting ('There are two problems here — first...') orients the listener. Persuasion structure: Ethos (credibility), Pathos (emotion), Logos (logic) — Aristotle's triad still governs.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Weak: 'We analyzed the data, ran three models, considered alternatives, and after careful review concluded we should exit the market.' Strong: 'We should exit the market. Three reasons: margins are negative, the trend is worsening, and reinvestment yields more elsewhere.' Same content, opposite impact.

PRACTICE: 1) Rewrite an email using BLUF. 2) Structure an argument in exactly three supporting points. 3) Identify ethos/pathos/logos in a persuasive piece you admire.

title: Difficult Conversations & Conflict
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Every difficult conversation has three layers (Stone/Patton/Heen): the What Happened conversation, the Feelings conversation, and the Identity conversation. Most people fight over facts while the real conflict is identity ('am I competent? am I a good person?'). Nonviolent Communication (Rosenberg): Observation → Feeling → Need → Request, without evaluation or blame. Separate impact from intent — 'you hurt me' is valid; 'you meant to hurt me' is a guess.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Instead of 'You're always late and it's disrespectful' (blame, identity attack), NVC gives: 'When the meeting started 15 minutes late (observation), I felt frustrated (feeling) because I needed the full hour to decide (need). Could we start on time going forward? (request).' Same message, no defensiveness triggered.

PRACTICE: 1) Convert a blame statement into NVC form. 2) Identify the identity issue beneath a recent conflict. 3) Practice separating impact from intent in a real disagreement.

title: Presenting & Public Speaking
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Structure beats charisma. Open with a hook (question, story, or surprising fact), state your thesis within 60 seconds, deliver three supporting sections, close with a call to action. Slides support you; they are not your notes — one idea per slide, minimal text. Nerves are physiological, not moral: reframe arousal as excitement rather than fear (Brooks' reappraisal research). Pausing is powerful — silence signals confidence and gives listeners time to absorb.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A speaker fills every silence with 'um' out of anxiety. Replacing filler with a two-second pause immediately reads as authority rather than nervousness — the same information, delivered with confidence, is received completely differently.

PRACTICE: 1) Write a 60-second opening with a hook and thesis. 2) Reduce a text-heavy slide to one idea. 3) Record yourself and count filler words; re-record replacing them with pauses.

title: Written Communication & Influence at Distance
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Writing is asynchronous influence — it must work without your presence. Clarity rules: short sentences, active voice ('the team missed the deadline' not 'the deadline was missed'), concrete nouns over abstractions. The inverted pyramid (journalism): most important information first, detail descending. Email discipline: one topic, clear subject line, explicit ask, deadline. In writing, ambiguity compounds — every unclear sentence multiplies across every reader.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Subject 'Update' with three paragraphs and a buried request gets ignored. Subject 'Decision needed by Thu: vendor选择' with the ask in line one gets answered. The information is identical; only the packaging changed the outcome.

PRACTICE: 1) Rewrite a passive-voice paragraph in active voice. 2) Restructure a rambling email using the inverted pyramid. 3) Write three subject lines that state the ask and deadline.

title: Executive Communication & Stakeholder Management
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Executives buy outcomes, not process — lead with impact, not effort. The 'so what?' test: every statement must survive the question. Tailor to the audience's decision: what do they need to decide, and what do they need to know to decide it? Manage stakeholders by mapping power × interest: high power/high interest = manage closely; low/low = monitor. Escalation is not failure; late escalation is. Communicating bad news early preserves credibility; hiding it destroys it permanently.

WORKED EXAMPLE: An engineer reports 'we refactored the auth module and improved test coverage.' The executive hears nothing actionable. Reframed: 'Login failures dropped 90%, which removes the top support cost.' Same work, translated into the currency the audience actually values.

PRACTICE: 1) Apply the 'so what?' test to five status statements. 2) Map your stakeholders on power × interest. 3) Rewrite a technical update in outcome language.

title: Grandmaster — Narrative & Organizational Communication
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At scale, leaders don't communicate messages — they build narratives. A narrative is a repeated, coherent story that explains where we are, where we're going, and why it matters. Repetition is not redundancy: a message must be heard many times before it's internalized; leaders quit repeating long before audiences absorb. Communication cascades break at each layer — what the CEO says is not what the frontline hears. Channel selection matters: sensitive news in person, decisions in writing, culture in stories.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A CEO announces a strategy once and assumes it landed. Six months later, no one can articulate it. The fix isn't a better speech — it's the same message, repeated consistently across every channel and every leader, for months. Consistency over eloquence.

PRACTICE: 1) Write your organization's narrative in three sentences. 2) Identify where your communication cascade breaks. 3) Design a repetition plan for one key message.

title: King Level — Communication as Leadership
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, communication IS leadership — an organization can only become what its leaders can articulate. Framing determines reality: whoever names the problem controls the solution space. Symbolic acts communicate more powerfully than statements — what leaders spend time on, tolerate, and reward is the real message. Psychological safety (Edmondson) is created or destroyed by how leaders respond to bad news and dissent. The King-level insight: your communication is not what you say; it is what people believe after you leave the room.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A leader declares 'we value candor,' then visibly bristles when challenged. The behavior overrides the statement instantly, and candor dies. Conversely, a leader who publicly thanks someone for delivering unwelcome news teaches the entire organization that truth is safe — one act communicates more than a year of memos.

PRACTICE: 1) List what your calendar and rewards communicate about your real priorities. 2) Reframe a problem in your organization and observe how the solution space shifts. 3) Design one symbolic act that would make your stated value credible.
